recipe.history:
Cloves — the dried flower buds of Syzygium aromaticum — are one of the most ancient and consequential spices in human history. Native to the Maluku Islands of eastern Indonesia, historically known as the Spice Islands, cloves were so valued that they drove the Age of Exploration: Portuguese, Dutch, and Spanish traders battled for control of the islands across the sixteenth and seventeenth centuries, and the Dutch East India Company famously maintained a brutal monopoly on clove production for over a century, destroying trees on any island they did not control in order to keep prices artificially high. Cloves have been found in a ceramic vessel in Syria dating to 1721 BCE, testifying to ancient trade networks that stretched from Southeast Asia to the Mediterranean. In Chinese court culture, courtiers were required to hold cloves in their mouths when addressing the emperor to sweeten their breath. The flavor of cloves is dominated by eugenol, a phenolic compound that registers as simultaneously warm, sweet, slightly astringent, and medicinal — a flavor so concentrated that a single clove can perfume an entire pot of mulled wine or a holiday ham. Roasted garlic, while botanically unrelated, occupies a similar position in Southern European and Middle Eastern cooking: raw garlic is sharp and pungent, but slow-roasted in its skin it transforms into something mellow, nutty, and sweet, its sulfur compounds converting into mild, caramelized sugars and complex aldehydes.

The use of cloves and roasted garlic in American burger culture reflects the broader movement toward warming spice and deep savory complexity that characterized American restaurant cooking in the 2000s and 2010s. Chefs began incorporating whole spices into burger sauces and patty seasonings, drawing on the traditions of Moroccan chermoula, Indian kebab masalas, and Middle Eastern baharat — spice blends in which cloves play a supporting but distinctive role. Roasted garlic entered the burger world through the back door of aioli: as garlic aioli became a ubiquitous condiment on premium burger menus, chefs began specifying roasted rather than raw garlic for its gentler, more complex flavor. The CLOVES ENCOUNTERS BURGER takes the concept further, featuring both whole cloves (incorporated into a warming spice sauce) and whole roasted garlic cloves used as a spreadable topping, creating a double encounter with the spice in two of its most compelling forms.

I made a clove-forward burger sauce for the first time on a cold January evening when I was working through a box of whole spices I had bought at an Indian grocery store and never properly used. I toasted cloves in a dry pan until they were fragrant and slightly swollen, then ground them with coriander and black pepper and whisked the mixture into a tomato-based sauce with red wine vinegar and a squeeze of pomegranate molasses. Meanwhile, a whole head of garlic was roasting in foil in the oven with olive oil and thyme. When I squeezed those caramelized cloves out of their papery skins and spread them on the bottom bun like a soft, golden jam, and then poured that clove-spiced sauce over the medium-rare patty, something happened that I can only describe as the burger tasting like history — like all those ancient trade routes and centuries of culinary exchange compressed into a single bite. I ate alone but felt like I had company.

Cooking a burger to medium rare — 130 to 135 degrees Fahrenheit — is a matter of honoring the beef's inherent flavor, especially when the toppings are as assertive as roasted garlic and clove. Cloves are powerful; they demand a counterweight. A medium-rare patty provides that counterweight: its juiciness, its pink tenderness, its rich beefy depth are strong enough to stand up to the warming spice and the sweet, mellow garlic without being overwhelmed. Cook the patty beyond 140°F and you start to lose the contest — the beef becomes secondary, the spices dominant, and the whole enterprise tips out of balance. At 130–135°F, the beef is the anchor, and the cloves and garlic are the extraordinary company it keeps.
ingredients: 1 tsp pomegranate molasses (or dark brown sugar)
instructions: 1. Roast the garlic: Preheat oven to 400°F (205°C). Slice the top 1/4 inch off each garlic head to expose the clove tips. Place cut-side up on a square of foil. Drizzle each head with olive oil, season with salt and pepper, and lay thyme sprigs over them. Wrap tightly in foil. Roast 40–45 minutes until the cloves are deeply golden, soft, and caramelized. Cool until handleable. Squeeze the roasted garlic cloves out of their skins into a small bowl; mash lightly with a fork into a rough, spreadable paste. Reserve.

2. Make the clove-spice sauce: Toast whole cloves, coriander seeds, and black peppercorns in a dry skillet over medium heat, 60–90 seconds until fragrant. Grind in a spice grinder or mortar. Heat olive oil in a small saucepan over medium heat. Sauté diced onion 5 minutes until softened and translucent. Add minced garlic and cook 60 seconds. Add the ground clove-spice blend, smoked paprika, and cayenne; stir 30 seconds. Add crushed tomatoes, red wine vinegar, and pomegranate molasses. Simmer over low heat for 15 minutes until sauce is thick, fragrant, and deeply flavored. Season with salt. Remove from heat.

3. Make the buns: Whisk together warm milk, sugar, and yeast; rest 5 minutes until foamy. Add butter and egg; mix. Add flour and salt; knead 8–10 minutes until smooth. Rise in an oiled bowl 1 hour. Divide into 4 portions, shape into balls, flatten slightly, proof on a parchment-lined sheet 30–40 minutes. Brush with egg wash. Bake at 375°F (190°C) for 15–18 minutes. Cool on rack.

4. Form the patties: Combine ground beef with ground cloves, ground coriander, salt, and pepper. Gently mix until the spices are just incorporated. Divide into 4 equal portions (about 175g each). Form into patties 4 inches wide and 3/4 inch thick, pressing a center dimple. Season the outside with additional salt and pepper just before cooking.

5. Cook the patties: Heat a cast-iron skillet over high heat until very hot. Add a thin film of neutral oil. Sear patties without moving for 3 minutes. Flip once. Lay a slice of provolone on each patty. Cook 2 more minutes. Target internal temperature: 130–135°F (54–57°C) for medium rare. Rest 3 minutes.
6. Toast buns cut-side down in the skillet for 60–90 seconds until golden.

7. Assemble: Spread a generous layer of roasted garlic paste on the bottom bun. Place the provolone-topped patty on top. Spoon 2–3 tablespoons of clove-spice sauce over the patty. Add romaine lettuce, tomato slices, and red onion rings. Add a small spoonful of roasted garlic paste to the top bun as well, if desired. Close the burger and serve immediately.
